items.readable_text:
Content:
The side-angle-side (SAS) congruence criterion can be used as a shortcut to prove that two triangles are congruent. It states the following.

Content:
> Two triangles are congruent if and only if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are congruent to two sides and the included angle of the other triangle.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the triangles below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a7d87e31cd1f9961b68e0ba951f308ed]

Content:
We can see that two sides of [MATH: \triangle ABC] are congruent to two sides of [MATH: \triangle KLM\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \overline{AB}\cong \overline{KL}, \quad
\overline{BC}\cong \overline{LM}.]
Also, we see that the included angles are congruent:
[MATH: \angle{B}\cong \angle{L}.]

Content:
Therefore, the SAS congruence criterion guarantees that these two triangles are congruent, and we can write

Content:
[MATH: \triangle ABC \cong \triangle KLM.]

Content:
Caution: When using the SAS criterion, it's vital to make sure that the angles you compare are the included angles between the two pairs of congruent sides. The SAS criterion only works if the included angles are congruent.

items.title: Identifying Congruent Triangles Using the SAS Criterion

sections.normalized_html: According to the SAS criterion only, which of the following triangles are congruent to [MATH: \mathcal{T}?]
sections.readable_text:

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The SAS (side-angle-side) congruence criterion states the following:

Two triangles are congruent if and only if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are congruent to two sides and the included angle of the other triangle.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given triangles.

  • [MATH: \mathcal{P} \cong \mathcal{T}] by SAS since two sides and the included angle of one triangle are congruent to two sides and the included angle of the other triangle.

  • [MATH: \mathcal{Q}] is not congruent to [MATH: \mathcal{T}] by SAS since we don't have a pair of congruent angles.

  • [MATH: \mathcal{R} \cong \mathcal{T}] by SAS too, since two sides and the included angle of one triangle are congruent to two sides and the included angle of the other triangle.

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: \mathcal{P}] and [MATH: \mathcal{R}] only."

  • Statement III is true. Since the two triangles are congruent, the corresponding sides must be congruent too. Hence, we obtain [MATH: BC|= EF; 2x|= x + 2; x|= 2.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The side-angle-side (SAS) congruence criterion can be used as a shortcut to prove that two triangles are congruent. It states the following.

Content:
> Two triangles are congruent if and only if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are congruent to two sides and the included angle of the other triangle.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the triangles below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a7d87e31cd1f9961b68e0ba951f308ed]

Content:
We can see that two sides of [MATH: \triangle ABC] are congruent to two sides of [MATH: \triangle KLM\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \overline{AB}\cong \overline{KL}, \quad
\overline{BC}\cong \overline{LM}.]
Also, we see that the included angles are congruent:
[MATH: \angle{B}\cong \angle{L}.]

Content:
Therefore, the SAS congruence criterion guarantees that these two triangles are congruent, and we can write

Content:
[MATH: \triangle ABC \cong \triangle KLM.]

Content:
Caution: When using the SAS criterion, it's vital to make sure that the angles you compare are the included angles between the two pairs of congruent sides. The SAS criterion only works if the included angles are congruent.

---
